Those statements describe ambitions announced at that time, not proof that the goals have already been achieved. Buyers assessing progress should look for subsequent reporting with clear scope and comparable measures. Manufacturers can make those commitments more useful by publishing progress against a consistent baseline, identifying which operations are covered and explaining setbacks as well as improvements. Accessible reporting lets buyers and communities distinguish a new promise from work already completed. A 2050 target is a direction of travel; annual evidence is what makes progress assessable. Public agencies and retailers also influence whether responsible disposal is affordable and convenient. The EPA’s 2025 used-tire guide identifies low-cost disposal alternatives and community education as tools for preventing dumping. For households, clear opening hours, eligibility rules and upfront fees can turn a good intention into a completed drop-off. Access belongs in the environmental discussion alongside recycling technology. Frequently asked questions Can I keep my tires longer to reduce waste Only while they remain safe and suitable for use. Follow the vehicle’s maintenance guidance and have concerns about damage or wear assessed. Waste prevention means avoiding premature deterioration, not postponing a replacement that is needed for safety. Where can I recycle old tires without paying too much Ask the replacement shop whether removal and handling are included in its quote, then compare local waste-agency collection options. Some communities offer free residential events. Confirm eligibility, tire types, quantity limits, fees and transport rules before making the trip. Are tires labeled eco friendly automatically a better choice No broad label establishes lower impact across the full life cycle. Ask whether the claim concerns materials, manufacturing, energy use while driving or recovery after use, and what evidence supports the comparison. Vehicle suitability and documented performance still matter. Reduce waste without passing the cost to households Reducing tire waste works best when the affordable choice is also a responsible one: maintain the tires already in service, compare the complete cost of suitable replacements, and arrange a clear route for the old set. At the next service visit, ask the shop to put the tire assessment, installed price and disposal arrangements in writing. That turns a broad environmental intention into a decision a household can actually make. Drivers can make those choices, but they cannot redesign a factory or build a collection network. Manufacturers must demonstrate progress, and communities need accessible recovery options. Lasting waste reduction depends on both: helping families avoid unnecessary purchases while making the tires that do need replacing part of a better-managed system.

articles.title: Halloween Streetwear Sale
articles.author: Tiqua Jackson
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Halloween is more than costumes and decorations. For many streetwear fans, it is also a chance to experiment with darker colours, bold graphics, oversized layers, and statement pieces. As Halloween approaches, the right outfit can help create a strong look without feeling uncomfortable or overly complicated. This season, the combination of Saint Michael Clothing and Chrome Hearts Clothing offers plenty of inspiration for people who enjoy expressive streetwear. From graphic hoodies and relaxed shirts to layered outfits and darker everyday pieces, these styles can work for Halloween events as well as regular autumn and winter outfits. With Halloween sales also becoming a popular time to refresh a wardrobe, shoppers can look for pieces that offer more than one-season appeal. Instead of buying something that can only be worn once, a well-chosen hoodie, shirt, or streetwear layer can become part of an everyday wardrobe. Why Streetwear Works So Well for Halloween Traditional Halloween outfits often focus on costumes, but streetwear gives people another way to create a seasonal look. Dark colours, bold artwork, oversized silhouettes, and layered clothing naturally fit the Halloween atmosphere. A black or dark-toned hoodie can be a simple starting point. Add relaxed trousers, a graphic shirt, and suitable footwear, and the outfit can quickly become more interesting without requiring a full costume. This approach is especially useful for people who want to enjoy Halloween while keeping their personal style. A good Halloween streetwear outfit should feel like something you would actually wear, rather than a costume that sits in the wardrobe after one night. The current interest in streetwear also makes Halloween a good opportunity to mix casual clothing with more expressive fashion choices. Saint Michael Clothing for Halloween Outfits Saint Michael Clothing Brand has a strong connection with graphic-focused streetwear aesthetics. Hoodies, shirts, and other casual pieces can provide an easy foundation for a Halloween-inspired outfit. For a simple look, start with a dark Saint Michael hoodie and pair it with black or washed trousers. Neutral sneakers can keep the outfit casual, while boots can create a heavier autumn feel. A graphic hoodie can also work as the main statement piece. Rather than adding too many accessories, allow the artwork and shape of the hoodie to stand out. This creates a cleaner outfit while still giving it a strong Halloween mood. For people attending a casual Halloween gathering, a Saint Michael shirt can also work well under an open jacket or oversized hoodie. Layering gives the outfit more depth and allows you to adjust your clothing depending on the weather. Chrome Hearts Clothing and Dark Street Style Chrome Hearts Clothing is another natural choice for people who prefer bold, darker streetwear. Its distinctive visual identity makes it easy to build outfits around statement shirts, hoodies, long sleeves, and other casual layers. A Chrome Hearts hoodie Halloween outfit can be kept simple with dark trousers and classic sneakers. The hoodie becomes the centre of attention while the rest of the outfit stays understated. For a slightly more layered appearance, try a long-sleeve shirt underneath a jacket or oversized outer layer. This works particularly well when temperatures begin to drop during the Halloween season. Chrome Hearts-inspired styling can also be adapted for daytime outfits. A graphic shirt with relaxed denim creates a casual streetwear look, while adding a darker jacket can make it more suitable for evening events. Halloween Streetwear Outfits Do Not Need to Be Complicated One of the easiest mistakes when planning a Halloween outfit is trying to add too many elements. A strong outfit does not necessarily require a costume, multiple accessories, or bright colours. Instead, focus on a few key pieces. A dark hoodie, relaxed trousers, and comfortable shoes can already create a suitable Halloween streetwear outfit. If you want more personality, add a graphic shirt, statement jacket, cap, or simple accessory. Colour also plays an important role. Black, charcoal, grey, washed tones, deep red, and muted colours can create a seasonal appearance without making the outfit look like a traditional costume. The benefit of this approach is that the same clothing can be worn after Halloween. That makes it easier to build a wardrobe around pieces you genuinely enjoy. How to Style a Saint Michael Hoodie for Halloween A Saint Michael hoodie Halloween outfit can be styled in several simple ways. For a relaxed daytime look, combine a hoodie with loose-fit jeans and everyday sneakers. If the weather is colder, add a jacket over the hoodie and choose darker trousers. For an evening Halloween event, black jeans or cargo trousers can create a stronger look. Boots can also add a more rugged appearance. You can also use layering to change the outfit without buying completely new pieces. Wear a graphic T-shirt under the hoodie, or place a lightweight jacket over it. Small changes can make the same hoodie feel different. The most important part is balance. If the hoodie has a large graphic design, keep the rest of the outfit relatively simple so the main piece remains noticeable. How to Create a Chrome Hearts Halloween Look Creating a Chrome Hearts Halloween outfit can also be straightforward. Start with one statement item and build around it. For example, a dark Chrome Hearts shirt can be paired with black denim and simple sneakers. For colder evenings, add a hoodie or jacket as an extra layer. A long-sleeve piece can work especially well for Halloween street style because it gives you more options for layering. You can wear it under a jacket or oversized shirt while keeping the outfit comfortable. Accessories can also be used, but they do not need to dominate the look. A simple cap, chain, or bag can complete the outfit without taking attention away from the clothing. Halloween Sale: Look for Pieces You Can Wear Again Halloween sales can be a useful opportunity to refresh a streetwear wardrobe, but it is worth thinking beyond the event itself. Instead of choosing something only because it looks Halloween-themed, consider whether you would wear it throughout the year. Hoodies, shirts, sweatshirts, jackets, and relaxed trousers can all become useful everyday pieces. A Saint Michael Halloween sale or Chrome Hearts Halloween sale can therefore be approached as a chance to find versatile streetwear rather than simply buying a seasonal costume. Look for colours and designs that match the rest of your wardrobe. A black hoodie, for example, can work for Halloween but also for casual weekends, travel, social events, and everyday outfits. This makes the purchase more practical and gives the clothing a longer life in your wardrobe. Mixing Saint Michael and Chrome Hearts Styles Streetwear does not always need to follow one brand from head to toe. You can take inspiration from different aesthetics and create a look that feels personal. For example, a Saint Michael graphic hoodie can be combined with simple pieces inspired by the darker Chrome Hearts streetwear aesthetic. Alternatively, a Chrome Hearts shirt can become the main piece while neutral layers keep the outfit balanced. When mixing styles, avoid making every item a statement. Choose one or two pieces that attract attention and keep the remaining clothing simple. This approach makes the outfit feel more natural and easier to wear. Halloween Street Style for Different Events Your Halloween outfit can change depending on where you are going. For a house party, a graphic hoodie and relaxed trousers can provide a comfortable option. For an outdoor event, layering becomes more important, especially when temperatures drop during the evening. For a casual dinner or social gathering, a graphic shirt with dark jeans and a jacket can create a cleaner appearance. If you are attending a larger Halloween event, you can make the outfit more noticeable with a statement hoodie, distinctive footwear, or carefully selected accessories. The key is to match your clothing to the occasion while keeping your personal style at the centre. Why Quality and Comfort Matter Halloween outfits often involve spending several hours walking, standing, meeting friends, or attending events. This makes comfort just as important as appearance. A hoodie or shirt should allow you to move easily. Comfortable trousers and suitable footwear can make a major difference during a long evening. Streetwear is particularly useful because relaxed fits and layering can provide both comfort and visual interest. Instead of choosing an outfit that looks good only in photographs, choose pieces you can comfortably wear for several hours. This is also why versatile clothing can be a better wardrobe investment than a single-use costume. Build Your Own Halloween Streetwear Style There is no single way to dress for Halloween. Some people prefer traditional costumes, while others enjoy creating a darker everyday streetwear look. If you prefer the second option, start with the basics. Choose a hoodie, shirt, jacket, or sweatshirt that reflects your style. Build the rest of the outfit around that piece using simple colours and comfortable fits. Saint Michael Clothing can provide inspiration for graphic-heavy and expressive looks, while Chrome Hearts Clothing can inspire darker and more distinctive streetwear combinations. The final result does not have to be complicated. A few carefully selected pieces can create a strong Halloween outfit while remaining useful throughout the rest of the year. Find Your Halloween Streetwear Look Halloween is a great time to experiment with streetwear and try combinations that you might not normally wear. Dark colours, graphic designs, oversized layers, and statement pieces can all help create a seasonal look without relying on a traditional costume. Whether you prefer a Saint Michael hoodie, a Chrome Hearts shirt, a layered streetwear outfit, or a simple dark-toned combination, the goal is to create a look that feels comfortable and authentic to your personal style. With Halloween sales offering another opportunity to explore new pieces, this season can be the perfect time to update your wardrobe with clothing that works beyond October. Choose versatile items, keep your outfit balanced, and let one or two standout pieces do the talking. A good Halloween outfit does not have to be complicated. Sometimes, the right hoodie, shirt, jacket, and pair of trousers are all you need to create a memorable streetwear look.

articles.title: A Fight for Workers’ Rights Turned the Tide in Brazil
articles.author: Cruz Bonlarron Martínez
articles.content: As Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva celebrated his historic victory over far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro on Sunday, he embraced trans congresswoman Erika Hilton and kissed her on the cheek in celebration. The video circulated on social media, with many users pointing to it as evidence of Brazil’s acceptance of trans identity and the key role that the LGBTQ+ community plays within Lula’s coalition. It is important to note that Hilton and other LGBTQ+ politicians are more than simply a piece of a diverse coalition. They are the force behind a piece of legislation that will reduce the Brazilian workweek from forty-four to forty hours, a historic achievement that contributed to Lula’s victory and helped keep fascism at bay. Life Beyond Work One day in 2023, after finishing his shift, a pharmacy assistant in Rio de Janeiro called Rick Azevedo decided to record a video railing against the six-day work schedule to which much of the Brazilian working class are subject, including a disproportionate number of black workers. In the video, he referred to the 6 x 1, the colloquial name for this work regime, as a “modern form of slavery” and asked when the working class was going to make a revolution to put an end to it. Azevedo went on to note that if he, as a single man, had no time to do anything, he could only imagine how bad things are for others with kids. He ended the video with a call to revolt, warning that if ordinary workers like him did not organize behind the issue, things would never change. He originally archived the video, but after his manager called him in to work early the next day, he decided to post it on TikTok during his shift. The video quickly went viral, with thousands of interactions shortly after it was posted. Azevedo, who already had a following on TikTok for posts about pop culture and Beyoncé Knowles, received messages from others who felt the same way. In response, he founded the social movement Vida Além do Trabalho (VAT, “Life Beyond Work”), organizing first through live streams and WhatsApp groups, then through petitions to change the law. Azevedo, who had spent much of his life jumping from job to job but never finding enough time to finish formal university studies, became a movement leader overnight. The movement soon spread to other states and crowdfunded a protest in São Paulo to organize around the issue, gaining the attention of Erika Hilton, a rising star in the Socialism and Liberty Party (PSOL). Because of his newfound popularity, Azevedo decided to run for Rio’s City Council in 2024 with PSOL’s support, further popularizing the movement and solidifying his alliance with Erika Hilton. The Fight in Congress After the initial 2024 protests and news of Azevedo’s election in Rio, calls to change the workweek gained momentum and were taken up by some of Brazil’s progressive members of Congress. However, under Brazilian law, a change of this kind could not be made through a simple legislative process; it required an amendment to the Brazilian Constitution. In Brazil, a constitutional amendment requires one-third of members in both houses to sign on. This seemed very hard to achieve at the time because many of those in Congress belonged to right-wing and center-right parties that initially opposed the change. In February 2025, Hilton got 234 members of Congress to sign on to the constitutional amendment proposal, well over the third needed, allowing her to bring the amendment up for formal debate in Congress. The initial proposal also proved to be quite ambitious, calling for a thirty-six-hour workweek spread over four days without any cut to pay, which would have transformed Brazil’s labor regulations into some of the most progressive in Latin America. The thirty-six-hour workweek met opposition from sectors on the center and Right who chose to side with capital and oppose it. Azevedo’s VAT movement and the Brazilian labor movement mobilized around the demand on May 1, and President Lula made the end of the 6 x 1 work schedule a centerpiece in his May Day address in 2025. Lula stated that this change was necessary to build a balance between workers’ professional lives and their well-being. But despite the pressure, the legislation sat in Congress for the rest of 2025. In April 2026, the president sent his own proposal to Congress to keep the issue in the media cycle and continue putting pressure on the lower chamber. The End of 6 x 1 The combination of pressure from above and below worked, and in May the proposal finally passed the lower chamber and moved to the Senate. By this point, the reform had been modified so that it would establish a forty-hour workweek with two days off instead of the four-day workweek Hilton had initially proposed. The timing now meant that labor reform would be a key part of the national debate in Brazil’s presidential election. The right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro was a sitting senator at the time, and he felt obliged to support the proposed constitutional change for fear of losing working-class voters. This essentially meant conceding that the Right had been wrong to oppose the labor reform. After the first round of elections on October 4, it seemed that Bolsonaro’s compromise might have sufficed to shore up support for his candidacy, as he topped the polls and his far-right Liberal Party made significant gains in both houses of Congress. However, Rick Azevedo was elected to Congress on the same night, and Erika Hilton became the female deputy with the highest number of votes in Brazilian history: 1,596,472. This demonstrated how the fight for a shorter workweek connected with diverse sectors of the Brazilian electorate. On October 14, a week after the first round of the election, the Brazilian Senate voted 75–1 to end the forty-four-hour workweek. This promised a change to the lives of sixteen million Brazilians who previously had only one day off a week. Although the legislation that eventually passed was less ambitious than Hilton’s original proposal, it still lowered the work week to forty hours with two days off. This promises to empower millions of workers by making Brazil into one of the few countries in Latin America, a region where businesses are notorious for exploiting workers, to have a forty-hour week. Winning the Culture Wars The debate around the forty-hour week became a key space for Lula’s campaign to regain momentum after it initially fell behind Bolsonaro in the first round, shifting the focus to what was at stake for the Brazilian working class and the possibility of future reforms. The issue forced the Right to concede that Lula and his coalition had the best interests of workers at heart. Lula’s viral victory kiss. (Facebook) The debate also revealed the hypocrisy of the Right’s homophobic and transphobic rhetoric around the family, with a gay man and a trans woman leading the fight for working-class families to be able to spend more time together, get an education, and watch their children grow. Now, as Lula enters his fourth (and surely final) term, the global left should watch closely to learn how to take back the narrative from the Right and connect working-class interests with the diverse forms of oppression that workers face. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Iowa Locals Prevail in Recertification Elections
articles.content: Two UE locals prevailed in “recertification” elections covering four public-sector bargaining units in October. The elections are required by the punitive anti-union law passed by Iowa Republicans in 2017. Public-sector unions are required to win votes from a majority of the bargaining unit, not just those voting — a standard that few if any politicians could meet. The law not only requires recertification elections every two years, it also severely limits what unions can bargain over: wages are the only mandatory subject of bargaining — meaning it is the only issue that can be taken to arbitration. Arbitration awards for wages are capped at inflation, which makes it essentially impossible for workers to get ahead. Although the law was designed to destroy public-sector unions entirely, UE Locals 893 and 896-COGS have now prevailed in five recertification elections in a row. Local 896 represents approximately 1,500 graduate workers at the University of Iowa in Iowa City. Local 893 is an amalgamated local with state, county, and school district workers in multiple bargaining units. The three bargaining units recertified this year cover 2,000 state social workers and 400 state scientists, both in statewide bargaining units, and the Winneshiek County road crew in the northeast part of the state. articles.title: Another Detroit Socialist Is Heading to Congress
articles.author: Donavan McKinney
articles.content: In 2018, the election of two democratic socialists to the House of Representatives marked the beginning of a new political era. The socialist freshmen, both endorsed by the recently reinvigorated Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), were Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez from New York City and Rashida Tlaib, representing Michigan’s Twelfth Congressional District in Detroit. Eight years later, DSA boasts more than 120,000 members and politicians in elected offices across the country. And after a wave of Democratic primary victories earlier this year, democratic socialists are set to significantly grow their foothold in Congress in today’s general election. Among the likely socialist victors is Donavan McKinney, who is expected to win easily in Michigan’s deep-blue Thirteenth District in Detroit and join Tlaib in representing the Motor City in the House. Jacobin spoke to him about why he’s running and how growing up working class in Detroit shaped his politics. Sara Wexler Why are you running for Congress? Donavan McKinney I’m running to bring the urgency that this moment demands. Right now, I represent the poorest state house district in Michigan: $14,000 is the median income. If you divide that up by twelve months, that’s a little over $1,200 a month. And the average rents in our neighborhoods, if you’re lucky, start at $1,300. So that’s all your money down the drain, and you’ve got to worry about the increase in the price of gas and groceries, and insurance costs, whether it’s health insurance or auto insurance. We have some of the highest auto insurance rates in the country. Then childcare costs as well and so many day-to-day expenses. I’m running to represent one of the five poorest congressional districts in the country. What I’m going through on the state level is the same thing. [Being in Congress will mean representing] bigger communities, a lot more people. However, it’s the same narrative — the same story: “I just don’t have enough resources to make ends meet.” So for me, this is about meeting the moment, getting people in these positions who are going to put working families first and put our district first. Sara Wexler Can you tell me about your campaign platform? What priorities are you running on? Donavan McKinney Universal childcare, Medicare for All, and getting big corporate money out of politics. First, I talk about universal childcare a lot as a state legislator. I coled the movement for Pre-K for all. We have pretty much universal pre-K in Michigan now because of our advocacy and the advocacy of many others. We want to expand that to childcare across the board; we’ll take the fight to Washington, DC, for universal childcare. For my wife and I, that’s the biggest expense in our day-to-day lives, because we have three beautiful children — two boys, four and two, and a baby girl who just turned one. We pay more for childcare for one of our children than we do for our whole mortgage. And you’ve got to think about how impoverished my district is. If we’re living paycheck to paycheck off of childcare alone, I don’t know how everybody else is getting through it. Second, Medicare for All: I’m a big believer because of my mom and what she had to go through. When I was an undergrad at the University of Michigan, I got a call from my mom panicking because she was rushed to the hospital emergency room and they had to do emergency brain surgery. She comes to find out that she had brain tumors growing. And at the time, the only way she could get health care was through her employer; she was working at the time, but her employer didn’t offer it. So she was uninsured. And they did the emergency surgery, but guess what? She got that big six-figure bill for that procedure, and she didn’t have any way to pay it. They put her on a payment plan, but I had to go work three jobs at the time while I was a full-time student to make sure that she got the care she needed. By the grace of God, the Affordable Care Act (ACA) kicked in not too long after that, and she was able to afford health care. But I’m a big believer in Medicare for All, because she had preexisting conditions. Whether you have a preexisting condition or not, you deserve health care. That’s why I’m a big proponent of Medicare for All. There [are so many problems] when it comes to ACA premiums, as well as my seniors on fixed incomes, rubbing pennies together to try to figure out if they should have food on their table for the day or pay more out of pocket for their doctor’s visits and skyrocketing costs when it comes to lifesaving prescription drugs. The third thing I talked about is getting money out of politics. I’ve led that initiative here at the state level. I’ve introduced that legislation two times since I’ve been in office, in back-to-back terms. Each term, we got more and more people. I think the first term we had fewer than ten people sign on. This time around, when we introduced it last year in the state legislature, I think we had thirty or forty people sign on. Now, if you look at every Democrat who’s running for state legislative office here in Michigan, they signed on to the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics initiative. We couldn’t get a hearing in the state house. So organizations and people on the ground decided to take back our power over legislation and create a ballot initiative. They collected six hundred thousand signatures across the state, and that initiative will be on the November 3 ballot. I’m excited about it, because it targets monopoly utility companies, our public utilities, as well as our insurance companies — health insurance companies and auto insurance — which give a lot of money to state legislators to really bend the needle toward them instead of working people. I’m looking to do the same thing federally, to sign onto the legislation of Congresswoman Summer Lee and Senator Bernie Sanders, which gets rid of all that dark super PAC money, as well as to overturn Citizens United . Those are my big three pillars. Sara Wexler You grew up working class in Detroit. Can you tell me a bit about your background and how that shaped your politics? Donavan McKinney I was born and grew up in Detroit, raised with my mom, my grandmother, and my younger brother. We moved thirteen times across the city; I spent the vast majority of my life in northeast Detroit, which I now represent in the state legislature. And if the general election goes well, I’ll be representing it in the halls of Congress. Like I said, we moved thirteen times. We stayed in cars, shelters, sometimes out in the street. We didn’t know where our next meal was going to come from, but there was no shortage of love and prayers that got us through those tough times. I remember what my grandmother told me growing up. She told me two things that I still live by today. Number one is count your blessings, because you woke up this morning when a lot of people didn’t. You have a roof over your head, clothes on your back, food on your table, and — we live in Detroit, the Motor City — a car to drive. Because our transit system isn’t that good yet, but we’re working on it; that’s something we’re going to take to DC to work on. But you’re able-bodied, you’ve got your mental health, you’ve got your faculties, things we take for granted day in and day out. Number two, she always used to say, “In life, there will always be people better off than you. There will always be people worse off than you, but never fight the urge to give.” And I put that quote on my first piece of literature when I first ran for state representative ten years ago, back in 2016 when I was just a bushy-tailed kid coming out of college, just trying to figure out life. I still live by those two principles today — they’re my North Star. That’s why I’m so passionate about working people and about the service, because that’s what’s forgotten in politics. [I like to say], politics is about the service of the people and bringing humanity and love and leading with your heart back into the politics, which [currently] is so divisive. There’s a lot of hatred, a lot of negativity, and we try to lead with love. Sara Wexler It seems like when you were growing up, people’s needs weren’t being met, and the affordability crisis was worsening, regardless of whether Democrats or Republicans were in power. What do you make of this? Donavan McKinney A lot of people I’ve talked to view the Democrats and the Republicans very similarly when it comes to economics. I do believe that the Democratic Party is the party of the people. I have seen the Democrats do a lot more than the Republicans in terms of [helping the] working class. But I’m a big believer in the Scripture. Scripture talks about how you can’t serve two masters. What is happening, especially now, is that the Dems are serving the corporate oligarchs, same as the Republicans. You’re either going to have to do what’s best and serve the interests of working people, or you’re going to serve the interests of just a few and increase the wealth of those who are taking advantage of regular working people. For me, we follow what we preach. That’s what people want to see. They want to see receipts. So look at our campaign: we ran a campaign that was people powered. We didn’t take a cent of corporate PAC money or AIPAC [American Israel Public Affairs Committee] money. A lot of our money came from individual people across our district, across our state, across our country, who believe in a different style of politics. Leading up to the primary, our average donation on ActBlue was around $30 or $32, something like that — tens of thousands of people just donating to a vision. I’m forever grateful for it, because we were outspent. My opponent [in the primary], the current congressman, had his own wealth. He made his money off of pharmaceuticals, and so he had his own money to put in. But he also took money from ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] contractors and AIPAC as well as other corporate PACs, crypto, all of that — DTE, our monopoly utility — and just lying on our name, putting a lot of ads out. I’m very grateful, by the grace of God, that people were really waking up and realizing, “You know what? Donovan is better for the job.” We’re bringing a message that resonates with people and brings folks together. Sara Wexler Before running for office, you worked for Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Healthcare Michigan, which is the state’s largest health care union. How has your experience with labor organizing informed your politics? Donavan McKinney I tell this story a lot about my grandfather. My grandfather passed away late last year during the campaign cycle. I’m trying to not be emotional, because the man taught me a lot. When I was a kid, he used to bring me to the union meetings a lot. He worked at Ford Motor Company in the Detroit metro region and was part of the United Auto Workers (UAW) for forty-two years. One of the most interesting things about my grandfather is that during those forty-two years, he never missed a day of work. I asked him at his retirement party some years ago, “Granddad, how did you do it?” He told me one thing that stood out, which was that he took pride in what he was doing. He knew that, with his bare hands, he was helping change a life or a family’s life. But more important, he knew that not only the union had his back, but that Ford Motor Company had his back. But fast-forward to the year 2026, that work that he had and that salary that he made — that dollar isn’t stretching as far. And these corporations have gotten greedier. Take, for instance, what happened at the Poletown plant in my district, which is on the border of Detroit and Hamtramck. It’s a General Motors factory plant. It’s nicknamed “Factory Zero.” It was the first factory in America, and the first factory in America to be net zero. It was really green, really environmentally friendly and forward-thinking around that. Earlier this year, they cut over a thousand jobs, all union jobs. They cut everybody’s jobs, and then, just a few months later, replaced them with robots. I talk about it in the union halls a lot; I talk about how much it’s bullsh–t and how, at the end of the day, nobody has our back but working people ourselves. We need to start electing folks with the right type of mindset and, more importantly, with the lived experience that [leads them to prioritize working people] over these greedy corporations. Sara Wexler That leads nicely into my next question. You’re running as a democratic socialist. What does that mean to you? Donavan McKinney I define politics as the redistribution of resources. That’s it; it’s black and white. If you’re in these positions of power and influence, if you’re not trying to figure out ways to bring home as many resources as possible back to your communities and the people you represent, then I need you to get up out of here. That’s what led me to run for Congress in the first place, because I felt like our current congressman wasn’t meeting the moment. We’re going to be able to pick up the phone and do constituent service work, because I understand what it’s like being on the phone trying to get somebody to answer to help when you’re in dire need. My current congressman is known for not picking up the phone, not doing the real constituent work of the job. Half the battle is showing up. The other half is trying to figure out resources to improve the quality of life of the people you represent. So in terms of democratic socialism, I’m a big believer in Dr Martin Luther King’s teachings. And Tupac [Shakur] said it best: “They got money for wars but can’t feed the poor.” You’re telling me we’re spending money for a war that nobody wants — a billion dollars a day in Iran. And you’re also telling me that, with H.R. 1 [the One Big Beautiful Bill Act], the Republican trifecta cut health care and food assistance for the most vulnerable populations across our country. And I thought Republicans didn’t believe in red tape: I thought they believed in slim government and lean government and achieving efficiency in government. But they want to hurt people in order to give a tax break to the wealthiest top 1-percent earners of our country. They’re telling people, “We want you to get recertified every six months for your health care. But we DOGEd government, and we know that you’re not going to get recertified in time because we don’t have the caseworkers to certify you in the right amount of time. Because of the savings we’re going to have on the back end from folks not being able to recertify, we’re going to give a tax break to the ultrawealthy.” That’s not the America I want to live in; that’s not the America people in my community want to live in, or anyone who I know wants to live in. It’s up to us Democrats to level the playing field and right the ship, so to speak. I’m going to push hard as hell and advocate for the poor folks in my communities. A lot of my community is struggling and they’re looking for somebody that’s going to fight for them, and that’s my job. Sara Wexler As you mentioned, you were able to oust the incumbent Democrat in your primary. I’m wondering what role different organizations, DSA for instance, have played in your campaign. Donavan McKinney I was quoted earlier in the campaign, and I said, “We’re building the biggest and baddest coalition in the country,” which is true. I’ve even had members of Congress call me because they’re like, “Yo, how did you do this?” We have some of the most established folks and even the most conservative Democrats endorsing our campaign, as well as all-the-way-to-the-left DSA types endorsing our campaign. I don’t know if it was just because of me or also because of how bad the incumbent was, but it’s because we’re speaking values. We’re leading with our heart, and we’re following what we’re preaching. We brought together faith leaders, elected officials from the federal, state, county, and local levels, community block club leaders, and unions. I was told I was the only nonincumbent the AFL-CIO endorsed on the federal level when it came to the Democratic primary. So we had the unions; we had groups like Justice Democrats and DSA and so many other great folks coming together and realizing that we deserve better. That was our campaign message: We deserve better. I’m so grateful because I couldn’t have done it without this coalition. I couldn’t have done it without people coming together and realizing that their voices matter and that they have the power to make a difference in our politics and change the trajectory of our country. We’re going to continue that movement as we get sworn in in January. It’s the inside-outside strategy that Dr King talked about. You need people on the outside agitating, advocating, but you also need people on the inside who are willing to listen, willing to really put those words to paper and move legislation very swiftly in this moment, with the urgency that it demands. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Trump Is Tearing It Apart
articles.author: Ted Vaill
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. For the past almost 70 years, I have been involved in politics, starting in 1957 when as a high school student I published in a national environmental magazine an article that called the U.S. national parks “America’s Wilderness Slums”. To his credit, President Eisenhower fixed this problem, which, of course, Trump is bringing back.As we reach the 2026 Midterms, I have the following random thoughts: We have to make sure that we never again have a President as morally corrupt and evil as Donald Trump. How do we do this? The Republican Party (I used to be a member) has to be destroyed or neutered so much by the voters that it changes its ways and returns to be the party it was in the 1960s (before Watergate) when I was the Legislative Assistant to a ranking Republican Congressman. We were the “loyal Opposition” to the Democratic majority. Today’s Republicans are often greedy, cruel pseudo-“patriots” who really are more like British loyalists than patriots like my ancestor Lt. Pelatiah Everett, who served under George Washington from 1775-1783. Where is the evidence that Trump is actually “winning” the Iran war? Almost all our “news” of the Iran war comes from military sources that may be doctored to show great successes like General Westmoreland did with the daily “body counts” he sent out from Vietnam (a war in which I served as a Navy JAG lawyer who opposed the war). By the way, I first opposed the Vietnam war in October, 1965, when the ranking Republican on the House Foreign Affairs Committee I worked for asked me to do a white paper on the pros and cons of the Vietnam War. I found 20 reasons why it was a bad idea and five why it was a good idea (two of which were later proved to be lies). Since then, I have always trusted my political judgment. That is why I believe that Trump must be and will be removed from office before he destroys our democracy. Related: Trump Denied Project 2025: Now He’s Carrying It Out By the time you read this, you should know if there is a “blue wave” returning the House and Senate to true opposition to the destruction of America that Trump has promulgated since January 20, 2025 with the help of the so-called Heritage Foundation. If the American voters decide that what Trump has done over the past 22 months is wonderful, it will cause a lot of us Democrats to leave the country or go underground to throw out Trump and his thugs. If there is a blue wave or even a blue tsunami, then America is on its way back to being a true democracy with the interests of its citizens, rich and poor, well and disabled, educated and less educated, addressed every day in Congress. I keep thinking of the brilliant Hans Christian Andersen’s story about “The Emperor Who Had No Clothes”. Donald Trump has shown that he has been walking around without wearing any clothes all his life, from the day in 1946 when he was born with a golden spoon in his mouth. And he grew up as a rich, racist bully who later used the teachings of his friend and advisor Roy Cohn to admit no wrong, deny everything, and to always hit below the belt. My ancestors have been fighting to create and preserve this country for the past 406 years, since my ancestor Gov. William Bradford landed at Plymouth on the Mayflower in 1620. My past 10 generations of Vaills and Everetts worked hard to make America what it is now, from fighting in the Revolutionary War, to being leaders of their Connecticut communities as ministers, to helping establish what is now a top college (Amherst), to inventing the the folding chair, to helping patent the radio tube and inventing the telegraph, to helping develop the Norden bombsight that destroyed Germany and ended World War lI. We are seven generations of college graduates, going back to Rev. Joseph Vaill, Dartmouth Class of 1778. Related: Trump’s Reichstag Fire And then there were the Drumpfs, who fled to America from Germany to escape the Kaiser’s military service and got rich from the brothels he ran in Seattle and the Klondike, to Donald’s father, conceived in Germany, who got rich building tenements in Brooklyn and Queens, gouged his poor tenants, at the same time as he attended KKK rallies and raised his son Donnie to care only for himself. And Donnie, how dare you spend your life stiffing your suppliers, cheating on your wives, and operating like a Mafia boss? You have no heart , and are a selfish son of a bitch. In fact, your mother was one of the immigrants (from Scotland) that you love to denigrate.7 . All of us know someone who is so self satisfied with their lives that they do not have an ounce of care for anyone outside their immediate family. All they care about is the stock market and how rich they and their family can get. They love to drive around in their Teslas. And they are proud to be Trumpsters. May they burn in hell…

articles.title: Life Beneath the Melting Glaciers
articles.author: Jaclynn Ashly
articles.content: Bulbul Kaie remembers when summer in Hassanabad revolved around a stream. The village lies in the mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan, a disputed territory in northern Pakistan bordering China, Afghanistan, and Indian-administered Kashmir. Kaie’s family would carry chairs down to the stream fed by meltwater from the glaciers above, where a cold breeze rose from the water. They would spend afternoons on its bank among orchards heavy with apricots and cherries. “We would sit together, drink tea, and enjoy the sound of the stream until it got dark,” recounts the mother of four. “We used to look forward to summer. The sound of the water made us feel calm.” Now summer brings dread. “We fear what will happen each year,” the fifty-year-old says. Pakistan has more than thirteen thousand glaciers, one of the largest concentrations outside the polar regions, many of them in Gilgit-Baltistan. As climate change drives temperatures higher in these mountains, where warming is outpacing the global average, the ice melts faster and rain falls harder and less predictably. Cloudbursts — intense, localized downpours that experts say were virtually unknown here until recently — can now destroy a village in an afternoon. Last year, Hassanabad was among dozens of villages across Gilgit-Baltistan hit by one of the region’s deadliest flood seasons in years. At least seventy-two people died , and more than a thousand homes were destroyed or damaged. The floods destroyed half of Kaie’s home. She has yet to rebuild. “I’m only staying here because I have no resources to go elsewhere,” she says, her voice breaking. “I fear for my children’s lives and mental health.” Bulbul Kaie sits with her twelve-year-old son inside their damaged home in Hassanabad, and a crack runs down the wall behind them. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) Kaie is one of thousands still trying to recover. Some live in tents or cracked houses they fear could collapse. Others have been moved onto bare government plots with no land to farm and no way to earn. Few can afford to start again, and the next disaster is rarely more than a season away. The people living among these glaciers bear almost no responsibility for the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming; Pakistan itself accounts for about 1 percent of global emissions. Yet it is among the countries most affected by extreme weather, and in its remote mountain communities, homes are being washed away, farmland is disappearing, and livelihoods are collapsing. At the Glaciers’ Mercy Behram Shah gathers cherries from a tree outside his Hassanabad home and carries them to the table in a woven basket. “We rely on the glaciers for everything,” says the seventy-six-year-old, who has lost about nine acres to floods in the past decade. “Our livelihoods, and even our drinking water, depend on them. We are completely at the mercy of these glaciers.” Every spring, before the summer melt, villagers would gather at the watercourses to pray over the year’s flow, asking God for protection and enough water for the months ahead, Shah recounts. These days, few still make the journey. “We used to see the glaciers as the source of our lives,” Shah says. “Now, because of the floods, we associate them with destruction.” Behram Shah at his home in Hassanabad. He lost about nine acres of land to floods in the past decade and says villagers are “completely at the mercy of these glaciers.” (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) “The cycles that kept us in balance for centuries are being disrupted,” he adds. “All we can do now is pray and leave everything to God.” Hassanabad sits in the Hunza Valley, in the Karakoram — one of four mountain ranges that meet in Gilgit-Baltistan and contain some of the world’s highest peaks. Its roughly 175 households are scattered across the mountainous terrain, clustered on either side of the stream and up the slopes. Most residents are Ismaili Muslims who farm fields and orchards passed down through generations. Three miles above the village, the Shisper and Muchuhar glaciers, once branches of a single glacier, eventually drain into the same stream, which runs about four miles down the valley to join the Hunza River. Their meltwater feeds the irrigation channels that keep Hassanabad alive. In 2018, the Shisper began to surge , exhibiting behavior of a type of glacier that can sit almost motionless for decades or centuries before suddenly lurching forward. It advanced nearly a mile, at one point moving nearly sixty feet a day, before pushing across the ravine and damming the stream draining the Muchuhar. The lake that formed behind the ice burst four times in four years, sending floodwater down the valley that scoured the ground along the stream’s banks. The last, in 2022, swept away the Karakoram Highway Bridge, cutting Hunza off from the rest of the country for two weeks. By last summer, the danger was supposed to have passed. The ice still lay across the ravine, says Sher Muhammad, a cryosphere scientist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, but a wide tunnel had opened through it and water was flowing freely. Then the heat came. One town in southern Gilgit-Baltistan hit 119 degrees Fahrenheit (48.3 degrees Celsius), its highest temperature in nearly three decades. Across the region, streams were already running high as unusually warm conditions accelerated snow and glacier melt. Chunks of ice broke off and fell into the stream, blocking the flow, Muhammad says. Water accumulated behind the ice blockages until they failed, releasing the impound water downstream. It happened twice, in July and August, damaging houses and farmland, ripping out a section of the Karakoram Highway, and cutting the water supply to Aliabad, Hunza’s main commercial town, and nearby villages. Over the years, dozens of homes in Hassanabad have been destroyed or dismantled before the floods could reach them. The Floodwater Threat What came before the floods, Kaie says, was not a roar. It was a silence. “It’s very ominous,” she says, sitting on the floor of her home, cracks running down the walls. “The entire flow of water suddenly feels like it stops. And there’s silence for about half an hour.” In those minutes, the family would run to the bank to see what was coming. If the water looked dangerous, Kaie would send the children uphill to a relative’s house and go back for whatever she could carry. “When the floodwater comes, it is so strong,” she says. “It carries boulders the size of houses. If it reaches your home, it will pull it from its foundations.” They have lived this way for years, fleeing when the water rises, returning when it drops. When I visited in August, the family had already fled several times that summer. Their fridge and other belongings were still at a relative’s house up the hill. Last year’s floods were the worst this part of Hassanabad had seen, residents say. They tore through the orchards between Kaie’s house and the stream and destroyed half the home she and her husband had spent seven years building. The couple had sold most of their farmland to afford it. The flood pathway in Hassanabad, with the stripped shells of dismantled homes along the edge of the canyon that floods have carved into the land. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) She scrolls through her phone to a photograph from before: rows of fruit trees running down to the water. “It was a very beautiful home,” she says, holding up the screen. Outside, the same ground is dry and stripped bare. Later, the highway was rebuilt. It had always run a couple of hundred feet below the houses until last summer’s flood swept away part of it. The rebuilt section was laid higher up the slope, directly in front of Kaie’s house. Now cargo trucks hauling goods between Pakistan and China pass a few feet from her door. They shake the walls, rattle the windows, and widen the cracks. Dust hangs in the air. Her twelve-year-old son sometimes wakes at night, hears the trucks, and thinks the flood has come back, she says. He runs outside, and the family has to find him in the dark. “This constant uncertainty is causing a lot of psychological issues for my children,” Kaie tells me, her son sitting quietly beside her. “I try to calm them down and assure them they are safe, but they are still terrified of every sound.” She wants to leave, but her husband drives someone else’s car for a living and does not earn enough to move elsewhere. And no one will buy a house in a village beset by recurrent floods. “If someone came and gave us money, we would leave immediately,” Kaie says, sniffling back tears. “It feels like torture knowing any day the waters will return and destroy our home we worked so hard to build. And it’s not a question of whether it will happen again; it’s guaranteed.” Other families have stopped waiting for the water. Each summer, they take their houses apart, carrying off beams, windows, and doors before the floods can claim them. Around the stream, the floods have carved a deep canyon into the land, with another Hassanabad neighborhood sitting beside it. On a flattened patch scattered with debris, the remains of the area’s jamatkhana , the Ismaili house of worship and community gathering, lie among the stripped shells of dismantled homes. Living on the Edge Sultan Ali, seventy-five, an elder and community leader, walks me along the cliff, shouting whenever I get too close to the edge. “The ground is not strong here,” he warns. “It can collapse at any moment.” He gestures at the canyon below. “You see all of this? This was the most beautiful part of our village,” he says, shaking his head. Nearby, Dilshad Bano, fifty-three, has come to pick cherries on a plot she abandoned about seven years ago. Floods destroyed half her house in 2019. The family dismantled the rest. “It took many years and a lot of hard work to build that house; we used up all our savings,” she says, standing in the ruins. “Then all of it was gone in a single day.” Dilshad Bano walks through the ruins of her home in Hassanabad. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) They have moved higher up the valley, to a house twenty-five minutes’ walk through the mountains from the nearest road. “When we have health problems, it becomes extremely difficult,” she tells me. Bano and her brother-in-law, Muhammad Abbas, fifty-five, each received about $900 in government compensation a few years ago, they say. Abbas’s four-room house is now a strip of orange-painted wall at the edge of the drop. Sultan Ali says the state needs to relocate families from the village, because the floods keep returning, and that residents have mostly relied on each other and on aid from the Aga Khan Development Network rather than the government. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) “That money was a joke,” he says. “You can’t rebuild your life with that.” He took out a bank loan and built three rooms at the far end of the village on the only plot he could afford. It floods and erodes like everywhere else. Beyond some compensation for affected families, officials have done little for Hassanabad, residents say. The state has evacuated families and sent food and medicine after each flood, and rebuilt the road and the bridge. But no one has been relocated, and residents say most of the assistance they received afterward — temporary shelters, food, and bathrooms — came from the Aga Khan Development Network. “The government is not helping us,” Ali says. “They need to relocate these families because this is a very dangerous place to live. We’re mostly farmers and shepherds and don’t have the resources to rebuild after losing everything.” There was supposed to be a warning, too. Hassanabad is one of two dozen valleys covered by GLOF-II, a UN Development Programme project with Pakistan’s climate ministry that installed weather stations, river gauges, and sirens across the north. During last summer’s floods, residents say, no sirens sounded. Muhammad, who was in Hunza at the time conducting a training session attended by officials from the meteorological department who manage the monitoring station, says the sirens are triggered when the water level reaches a predefined threshold. The stream in Hassanabad did not reach the threshold required to trigger the siren, he says. Residents say the siren on the bridge was later swept away by the flood. Villagers must rely on one another instead. On the hottest days, when the melt runs high, volunteers from the community post themselves along the stream. When they see dust rising from the ravine, a sign that water has broken loose upstream, they quickly warn residents. “Despite all these disasters and uncertainties, we are more united,” Ali says. “We all realize we are in the same situation, and we only have each other.” “My Enemy” Nargisa Khatoon was married in a mud and stone house, with carved wooden beams, that had stood for two centuries. “It was beautifully decorated,” says the eighty-three-year-old. Her family has lived for generations in Tokorkot, a village in the Nagar Valley across the Hunza River from Hassanabad. They were landowners under the mirs, the princes who ruled Nagar until Pakistan abolished the monarchy in the 1970s. In 2022, a summer of debris flows struck part of the house and swept away most of the family’s land and trees. For two years, they slept outdoors in a garden beneath a tarpaulin rigged against the rain and sun, or with relatives when there was room, before building the small house Khatoon lives in now. Nargisa Khatoon in Tokorkot, a village in the Nagar Valley. In 2022 debris flows swept away most of her family’s land, and trees and struck part of their two-hundred-year-old house, forcing them to sleep outdoors under a tarpaulin for two years. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) “I don’t like to remember that day,” she tells me, shuddering. “To see my home swallowed by the water, right in front of me. . . . I was shocked.” For months after, fear kept the village awake. People walked the riverbank at night, watching the water, wondering whose house would go next. “I still have dreams about those days,” she says. Khatoon grew up seeing the water as a blessing. It irrigated the fields and grew the walnut trees. “But after the floods destroyed everything around us, I became afraid of the water,” she explains, leaning against the side of her house. “Now, I see it as my enemy.” Unlike Hassanabad’s Ismailis, people here are Twelver Shia, the largest religious community in Gilgit-Baltistan. The village of a few dozen families sits where two waterways meet: the Hispar River and the Hopar Stream, which comes down from the glaciers of the Hopar Valley above. The village is hemmed in by flood-prone streams on either side and the river in front. Residents say there is nowhere to go. The Hopar Stream had flooded now and then for as long as anyone could remember. But in the summer of 2022, extreme heat followed by heavy rain likely destabilized the Daranchi Glacier, according to a study published last year, sending more than twenty debris flows — torrents of water, rock, and mud — down the stream in a single month, a frequency the researchers called unprecedented. The path of the debris flows through Tokorkot, a village in the Nagar Valley. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) Across Tokorkot and four other villages along the stream, at least twelve houses, schools, forty irrigation and water channels, bridges, and about seventy-five acres of farmland were swept away . The district administration sent some tents, according to residents, and families spent the rest of the summer in them. When the floods returned last year, destroying a bridge and cutting the road to Tokorkot, families took shelter in the same tents. On the hottest days, families still leave for higher ground, carrying food and sleeping together in tents. In Tokorkot, the fear is too much water. In the valley above, among farmers whose fields the glaciers feed, it is too little. Qurban Ali has watched the ice vanish over his lifetime. When the seventy-two-year-old farmer was young, his family worked fields low in the Hopar Valley, fed by meltwater from the Barpu Glacier. As the glacier thinned, its surface sank and the meltwater level fell with it, until the water dropped below the mouths of the irrigation channels that carried it to their fields. The family abandoned those fields and moved higher, onto land watered by the Daranchi — the glacier behind Tokorkot’s 2022 debris flows. “The glaciers are going deeper underground day by day,” he says. “So we cannot reach and bring up the water.” Farmers say the Daranchi is thinning too. Satellite measurements show the glaciers here losing mass every year since 2000, with the heaviest losses at their lower ends, where farmers draw their water. “Our entire life here revolves around the glacier water,” Ali tells me. “If there are no more glaciers, then there’s no more life.” Qurban Ali, a farmer in the Hopar Valley, has watched the Barpu glacier thin until its meltwater fell below the irrigation channels that fed his family’s fields, forcing them to abandon the land and move higher up to fields watered by the Daranchi Glacier, which is now thinning too. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) Hopar sits on a terrace of fields about 330 feet above the Bualtar glacier, known locally as Hopar. From a lookout at the head of the valley, its ice lies directly below, blackened with rock and dust. When a geographer surveyed Hopar in the mid-1980s, its five villages and roughly four thousand people were irrigating some seven hundred acres of terraces through more than 180 miles of hand-dug channels, with more meltwater than the fields needed for most of the growing season. Satellite records since 1993 show the snow and ice on the Hopar catchment shrinking by more than two-thirds, with the heaviest losses at the lower end of the glacier, where farmers draw their water. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) Satellite records since 1993 show the snow and ice in the catchment shrinking by more than two-thirds, and researchers have also documented fields in the valley being cut off from their water. Left With Nothing Rashida sits outside her tent and washes the family’s clothes by hand in water carried up from the Ghizer River, one of the region’s main rivers. It quickly turns brown with silt. She stops, takes a deep breath and wipes sweat from her forehead. “At our home in the village, we had a washing machine and clean running water,” the thirty-seven-year-old says. “I’m not used to living like this.” Rashida sits with her husband and daughters inside the tent that has been their home since last year. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) Rashida’s family has lived in this tent settlement since last year, when they were displaced from their village, Hakis Thingi, in the Gupis Valley of Ghizer district, in western Gilgit-Baltistan. At about 3 a.m. on August 22, a glacial lake in the mountains above Talidas village, in the Raushan area, burst . Officials blamed high temperatures. Water poured down a side stream, triggering landslides on both sides of the valley and sending a powerful debris flow through Talidas, flattening it. The debris then blocked the Ghizer River. For about six hours, the river stopped flowing as water backed up behind the blockage. By daylight, the ensuing lake was several miles long. Across six villages, the flood destroyed or damaged hundreds of houses and large tracts of land. It also submerged part of the only road connecting the area to the rest of the region. No one, however, was killed. Shepherds high in the mountains spotted the flood coming and phoned down to the villages below, where trained volunteers moved families out before the water arrived. About 80 percent of Talidas was destroyed . Upstream, the rising water swallowed houses in Hakis Thingi village and nearby settlements. More than three thousand people from 330 households were displaced — the second-largest displacement in Gilgit-Baltistan since the Attabad disaster in 2010, when a landslide dammed the Hunza River and submerged a string of villages. A year later, the floodwater in the Raushan area still stretches across parts of the valley, rooftops jutting above its surface. Submerged homes in the Raushan area. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) A resettlement site was built high in the mountains for some of those displaced from Talidas, isolated from the villages and services below. Residents say the government provided the land. The University of Lahore, a private university, funded the houses at about $720 each. Around sixty-five homes were washed away in Talidas, but only some families were provided plots, residents say. The rest are staying with relatives or in tents. About twenty-three families from Hakis Thingi, meanwhile, still live in a sprawling tent settlement across the river from their drowned village. Residents say the government has allocated each family about a twelfth of an acre, and aid organizations are providing materials for a one-room shelter with a kitchen and bathroom. But the families, who lost their land and livelihoods, must provide the labor themselves. The barren plots are only big enough for the shelters, residents say, and they cannot farm because the surrounding land is government-owned. They have relied on private aid, which dried up at the start of this year, and on whatever daily work they can find in construction, farming, or local shops. When I visited in August, not a single shelter was finished, and the entire community was still living in tents. “My whole life is different now,” Rashida says, settling onto the ground inside the tent beside her husband. Nowhere to Turn In Hakis Thingi, each family had scattered plots planted with almonds, apricots, apples, cherries, and mulberries. They grew their own vegetables, kept cows for milk and sold dried fruit at local markets for the cash they needed for clothes, household goods, and school fees. For Rashida, her children’s education mattered most. She says all of them did well at school. “Before, we could easily afford to send them to very good English-medium schools,” she tells me. “Now we have to ask [nongovernmental organizations] for help with the costs of government schools.” “I used to have very big plans for them,” she adds, as her children pull back the front of the tent and peek shyly inside. “I believed they would all go to university.” “Now I’m just worried about how to feed them each day.” Residents here say living so close to the Ghizer River — the river that took their homes — also leaves them constantly frightened. A couple of miles upstream, others never left. Their houses still stand on the edge of the lake. About twenty-four of their neighbors’ homes remain submerged, occasionally reappearing as the lake recedes. Water drains through a natural spillway in the debris and officials have declared the lake no longer a threat. Zarnisa, sixty, and her husband, Abdul Qayum, eighty, have moved between their home and the tents for more than a year. Their house stayed flooded for about six months, only its roof visible. When the water fell in January, they returned; three months later, it rose again. A few days before I met them, the spillway had widened, the lake dropped and they went home again. Zarnisa with her husband, Abdul Qayum, at their home on the edge of the lake in the Raushan area. They have moved between the house and tents on higher ground for more than a year. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) “We are always afraid,” Zarnisa says, guiding me to the edge of her small yard and pointing to the water just a few feet away. “Maybe in a few days the water will rise again, and we will have to flee.” Zarnisa’s husband has fallen into depression after being repeatedly displaced from their only home. “He’s constantly having panic attacks,” she tells me. From their yard, the roofs of sunken homes rise above the water, a perpetual reminder of what will eventually happen again to their own. “It gives me a lot of anxiety,” she says. More than her own house, however, she worries about the neighbors whose homes are already gone. “My neighbors were all like family to me. I’m always thinking about them and feeling sad.” Those neighbors now live in tents on higher ground or in the homes of relatives. They have not been given plots or shelters. One of them is thirty-five-year-old Zaibunisa. Her family owned three houses with shops attached, and she ran a small early education school for local children. All of it is now under the lake, along with their land. Zaibunisa outside the tent she pitched beside a relative’s house in the Gupis Valley. Her family’s three houses are now all under the lake. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) “When the flood came, we didn’t have time to grab anything, not even our phones,” Zaibunisa says. “We were left with nothing but our lives.” With no other land, she pitched a tent outside a relative’s house. “We feel stuck,” she tells me, standing outside the tent she shares with her husband and their three young children. “We need help.” “No Safe Area” About a week before the glacial flood, a different kind of disaster struck elsewhere in the Gupis valley. In Khalti village, the ground is a field of boulders and rocks. “Nobody here had ever feared floods; this side of the valley has no glacier above it,” says Karim Beig, seventy-three, a village elder. “The danger, in living memory, was always avalanches.” On August 14, cloudbursts hit thirty-seven locations across Ghizer. At least thirteen people died . These downpours can dump four inches of rain or more in an hour over an area just a few miles across, sending walls of water and mud down the slopes within minutes. One hit Khalti. Residents say eight houses were destroyed in about ten minutes and about four more were damaged. Six members of one seven-person family died. Villagers who reached the wreckage say they heard a small boy crying beneath it and dug him out. Beig and his younger brother, also in his seventies, lost half their house and most of their orchards and land. Beig leads me through the rubble, then crouches and motions for me to follow him down a crevice. A small backpack and other belongings lie beneath the debris, left behind by families whose homes were crushed by the rocks and floodwater. Cloudbursts are a “very new phenomenon” here, explains Syed Najam Hassan, an assistant professor at Karakoram International University in Gilgit who uses satellite data to map the region’s glacial lakes. They are associated with the monsoon, which until recently rarely reached these altitudes. Ghulam Rasul, former director general of the Pakistan Meteorological Department, says the mountains are warming faster than the plains below, strengthening the forces pushing the monsoon north. The Himalaya runs east to west, blocking its path. But toward the west, the wall of mountains ends, and the monsoon is now pushing through into the high Karakoram. “Now we all feel exposed,” Beig says, balancing on one of the rocks scattered across the village. “Every night when it rains, no one can sleep. Some of us come outside and watch the clouds for any sign of what might happen.” Karim Beig stands on the boulders left behind by the cloudburst in Khalti. He and his younger brother lost half their house and most of their orchards and land. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) Communities here have read the signs of approaching glacial floods for centuries, but nothing passed down by their elders tells them what a cloudburst looks like before it comes. Even researchers struggle to predict them, Najam says. A village can be sitting under clear skies while a storm builds over the ravine above, with the water arriving half an hour later. “Everything has changed since that day,” Beig says. “It’s like we’ve been invaded by something unfamiliar, something we don’t understand and that could attack us at any moment.” Theses dangers extend throughout the region. “Across Gilgit-Baltistan, everywhere is at high risk,” Najam tells me. “With the climate changing, there is no safe area.” The debris channel left by a cloudburst in Khalti village. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) While the water can eventually recede, the trauma cannot. Nargis Asad, who chairs the psychiatry department at Aga Khan University in Karachi and has studied the mental health of displaced people in Pakistan since the 2005 earthquake , says these communities are not recovering from a single disaster but living in a state of chronic exposure. “When you are continuously exposed to a threatening situation, there is an ongoing state of worry and apprehension about an impending disaster that can come at any time,” Asad explains. “It becomes a very fearful existence, affecting your psychological, cognitive, and physical well-being.” “Losing your livelihood and your source of income is also a real trauma,” she adds. “It is a major hit to your identity and creates a sense of helplessness, especially when it is land your family has lived on for generations.” The toll is physical, too, she says: cardiac problems, disrupted sleep, and illnesses that emerge long after the flood has receded. And the effects can extend to the next generation. “When children live under constant fear, their learning capacity, sense of safety, and sense of trust are all affected,” she says. Sher Wali and Jamali inside their worn tent at the Hakis Thingi camp. (Jaclynn Ashly / Jacobin ) At the camp for displaced families from Hakis Thingi, Sher Wali, ninety, sits in his worn tent with his wife, Jamali, sixty, grieving decades of lost work. “All my life, I worked to build on what my ancestors gave me, to give my children more than I had,” he says, his voice rough with exhaustion. “I lived off the land and cows and had a happy life,” he continues. “But now our children don’t even have milk for their tea or any fruit to eat.” He points through the tent opening to the treeless land outside, the sun beating down. At night, he takes stock of everything he lost in the floods. “I remember every section of my land, every fruit tree and every piece of property I no longer have,” he tells me. “It pains my heart, and I can’t sleep well.” “I’m an old man. . . . my life is almost over,” he adds. “But I fear for future generations. Without land or jobs, I’m afraid many of our young people and children will just be left to die.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
